questions.q: Name the three main supporting human characters or character-groups in "Journey to the End of the Earth" and state one key action or description associated with each from the text.
questions.a: Correct answer: (1) Geoff Green — Canadian head of Students on Ice, "got tired of carting celebrities and retired, rich, curiosity-seekers," now takes high school students to foster "new understanding and respect for our planet." (2) The Captain — of Akademik Shokalskiy, decides to turn back when ship wedges in ice, instructs all 52 to "climb down the gangplank and walk on the ocean." (3) The 52 students — "teenagers who still have the idealism to save the world," described as "future generation of policy-makers." A wrong answer that lists only "the captain and students" or adds "phytoplankton" or "seals" reveals the student cannot distinguish human supporting characters from environmental elements, or misses Geoff Green entirely — a critical omission because he articulates the programme's philosophy.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the author includes Geoff Green's backstory about "carting celebrities and retired, rich, curiosity-seekers" before describing his current work with students. What narrative purpose does this contrast serve?
questions.a: Correct answer: The contrast establishes Geoff Green as a character who has made a deliberate ethical shift — from facilitating passive, privileged tourism to enabling active, youth-driven education. It serves three narrative purposes: (1) It critiques superficial engagement with Antarctica (celebrities/rich tourists only "give back in a limited way"), (2) It positions students as agents of change ("ready to absorb, learn, and most importantly, act"), and (3) It reinforces the chapter's central argument that experiential education at a formative age is more valuable than late-stage awareness. A wrong answer that says "it shows he used to be a tour guide" or "it gives his biography" misses the thematic contrast — the student sees facts but not the author's argument about what kind of human presence Antarctica needs.

questions.q: The Captain orders everyone to "walk on the ocean" when the ship cannot proceed further. Using the PEEL structure (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link), write a 4-sentence analysis of what this moment reveals about the Captain's narrative function.
questions.a: Correct PEEL answer: Point — The Captain functions as a catalyst for the narrator's epiphany about planetary interconnectedness. Evidence — When the Shokalskiy wedges in ice at 65.55°S, he "decided we were going to turn around and head back north, but before we did, we were all instructed to climb down the gangplank and walk on the ocean." Explanation — By forcing the group onto the metre-thick ice pack above 180 metres of living salt water, he creates the physical conditions for the narrator's revelation: "everything does indeed connect." Link — This mirrors the chapter's geological message that human history is a "few seconds on the geological clock" — the Captain's practical decision becomes a philosophical threshold. A wrong answer that only describes the event ("he made them walk on ice") without linking to theme or the narrator's internal shift shows the student cannot move from plot summary to character-function analysis.

questions.q: Compare the narrative roles of Geoff Green and the Captain. Both are authority figures on the expedition, but they represent different relationships between humans and Antarctica. Analyze this contrast using two textual details for each character.
questions.a: Correct analysis: Geoff Green represents intentional, educational human presence — he "offers the future generation of policy-makers a life-changing experience" because "it's impossible to go anywhere near the South Pole and not be affected by it." His authority is pedagogical and future-oriented. The Captain represents operational, responsive human presence — he makes real-time safety decisions ("The Captain decided we were going to turn around") and enables direct physical encounter ("instructed to climb down... walk on the ocean"). His authority is immediate and nature-constrained. Contrast: Green chooses who comes and why (selection for impact); the Captain decides when they leave and how they experience the limit (submission to ice). Together they frame the expedition as both a designed intervention (Green) and a humbling encounter (Captain). A wrong answer that calls both "leaders" or "organizers" flattens the thematic distinction between proactive education and reactive humility — a distinction the text carefully builds.

questions.q: Evaluate this claim: "The 52 students are not characters but a collective symbol." Defend or refute using at least three textual references. Consider how the text individualizes or generalizes them.
questions.a: Correct evaluation: The claim is largely defensible. The text never names a single student, gives no individual dialogue, and describes them only as a group: "all 52 of us, kitted out in Gore-Tex and glares," "a bunch of teenagers who still have the idealism to save the world," "future generation of policy-makers." Three references confirm their symbolic function: (1) "headed by Canadian Geoff Green, who got tired of carting celebrities... With Students on Ice, he offers the future generation of policy-makers a life-changing experience" — they are the programme's purpose, not persons. (2) "when you can visibly see glaciers retreating... you begin to realise that the threat of global warming is very real" — the generic "you" applies to any student, not a specific one. (3) The closing reflection — "after spending two weeks with a bunch of teenagers who still have the idealism to save the world" — reduces them to an emblem of hope. However, the narrator includes herself in "all 52 of us," briefly blurring the line between protagonist and group. A wrong answer that says "they are characters because they are people" confuses ontological status with narrative function — in literary analysis, a group with no individuation operates as a symbol.

questions.q: Create a 60-word diary entry from the perspective of ONE student on the expedition, written the night after "walking on the ocean." The entry must reflect the chapter's themes (geological time, climate urgency, interconnectedness) and show the student's internal shift — without naming Geoff Green or the Captain.
questions.a: Strong answer criteria: (1) First-person voice of a teenager. (2) References the physical experience: ice under feet, 180m water below, seals, silence, 24-hour light. (3) Articulates a shift from abstract knowledge to visceral understanding — e.g., "I knew the ice held carbon records, but tonight I felt the planet breathing." (4) Connects to geological scale — "12,000 years is nothing." (5) Ends with resolve to act — "we have to be the generation that stops the melting." Weak answer: generic travel journal ("cold today, saw seals, walked on ice"), no thematic vocabulary (Gondwana, carbon, phytoplankton, geological clock), no internal change. A poor answer reveals the student cannot adopt the text's conceptual framework or distinguish tourist reaction from the narrator's epiphany.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Supporting characters in "Journey to the End of the Earth" are the individuals who accompany the narrator on the Antarctic expedition and whose roles, perspectives, and actions illuminate the chapter's central themes of climate change, geological history, and youth-led ______ action.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you're watching a documentary about a school trip to ______ — the narrator is the filmmaker, but the teacher leading the trip, the ship's captain, and the students themselves each represent a different argument about why this journey matters.
Fill in the blank: The ______ students aren't just passengers — they are the "future policy-makers" the text explicitly names.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to identify each supporting character, cite textual evidence for their role, explain how each character advances a specific theme (e.g., Geoff Green → education as activism; the Captain → human limits vs. nature; the students → generational responsibility), and write a structured 4-point answer comparing their.
